name: Hana Ito

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for any company, union, party or government. Everything you say stays confidential, and your name won't be attached to it. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work for a contractor that does the cable jobs for the power company in Eastbank, which is the river side of the city. A lot of my days are underground work now: digging out a pavement, finding a damaged cable, jointing it back together in a pit while the traffic goes past my ear. When there's a storm we all go out on the overhead lines too, sometimes sixteen hours straight. I like the jointing best, it's fiddly and quiet, like sewing with gloves on.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How long have you been doing it?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Twenty-six years. I came in late, at thirty-two, after a factory closed, and I was one of three women on the whole patch. Now there's a few more, which I'm proud of. I'm the women's rep for our union branch, mostly because nobody else would do it.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner Tomas runs a little bike repair shop on Canal Street that makes about enough to pay its own rent. Our son went through a divorce last year and we lent him most of what we had for a deposit on a flat. So right now there's maybe two weeks of bills in the bank. Contractor pay is lower than the company's own crews, and there aren't many other cable outfits round here.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, now let's talk about what actually matters, like staffing and pay. Half the hype was companies trying to scare us into accepting less. I'd probably post something like that in the branch group chat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, it's fine. I use one of those chat programs now and then to tidy up my incident reports, because my spelling is terrible, and that's about all it's good for. I'd keep going and hope the contract gets renewed next year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on, mainly. I'd keep chipping away at paying ourselves back, maybe a hundred a month once Ken starts returning some of the loan. And I'd keep pushing the contractor to match the company crews' pay, which is the fight I care about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, honestly. Like a normal Monday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the contract renewal. How much does that worry you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: More than AI does, if I'm honest. Every three years the power company puts the cable work out to tender and we all hold our breath. Last time a cheaper firm nearly got it and we'd have had to reapply for our own jobs at less money. My real fear every three years is the tender, not the robot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you use the chat program more if it stayed this modest?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably a bit. My daughter showed me how to ask it to explain a new safety rule in plain words, and that saved me a whole evening with the manual. But I'm not going to start asking it how to joint a cable.

S0.say: I'd say good, now let's talk about what matters, like staffing and pay. I'd post in the branch group chat that a lot of the hype was companies trying to scare us into accepting less.
S0.think: For me it changes very little, since I only use a chat program to tidy my reports. My real worry is the contract renewal every three years, not the technology.
S0.do: Carries on as normal and starts repaying their savings by about a hundred a month once her son returns some of the loan. Keeps pushing the contractor to match company crew pay.
S0.quote: My real fear every three years is the tender, not the robot.
S0.fieldNote: Hana's main pressure is the tender cycle, which already threatens her job every three years. She uses AI lightly and practically, for spelling and plain-language safety rules. Her politics come through as a steady focus on contractor pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the change has to be shared fairly. If the company saves money with new tools, some of that should come back as training and pay, not just dividends. That's what I'd say at work and that's what I'd say online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think the underground work is safer than the overhead stuff for a while. A robot in a muddy pit with old cables from the sixties, I can't see it soon. But the planning and the fault finding, that could go to software fast, and that's where the contractor would cut first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask for training on whatever new fault-finding kit came in, as soon as other crews had tried it and it worked. I'd get the branch to put training into the next contract talks. And I'd ask Ken to start paying back sooner, which won't be a fun conversation.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy. Not scared, but I'd be watching.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you trust a new tool enough to use it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Seeing it work for someone I know. When the cable locators with the screens came in, I waited till my mate Rosa had used one for six months. Then I picked it up and never looked back.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Ken about the loan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, love, things are changing at work and we need a cushion again, so can you start with fifty a month. He'd say yes, he's a good lad. It's me who hates asking.

S1.say: I'd say the change has to be shared fairly, with savings coming back to workers as training and pay rather than dividends. I'd say the same at work and online.
S1.think: I think underground work in muddy pits with old cables is safe for a while. The planning and fault finding could move to software fast, and that's where the contractor would cut.
S1.do: Asks for training on new fault-finding kit once other crews have proven it. Gets the union branch to put training into contract talks and asks her son to start repaying fifty a month.
S1.feel: Uneasy and watchful, but not scared.
S1.quote: A robot in a muddy pit with old cables from the sixties, I can't see it soon.
S1.fieldNote: She separates the parts of her job that are exposed from the parts that aren't, which gives her a measured view. She adopts tools once a colleague she trusts has proven them. Asking her son for money back is the hardest step for her personally.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this needs the government acting like it's an emergency, because it is. Pause it, regulate it, make the companies pay into a fund for the people they put out of work. I'd go on a march for that, and I've only been on two in my life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be sixty, with almost nothing saved and a partner whose shop barely pays. If the contractor loses the cable work to robots, there's no other cable firm to walk to. I'd be lying if I said I knew what we'd do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First month, I'd sit down with Tomas and go through every bill. The car would go, the gym would go. I'd ask the union what redundancy terms the contract gives us, and I'd look at whether the training centre needs instructors for the new kit, because someone has to teach it. Then I'd go on that march.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick, a bit. Like the moment in a storm when a pole goes down and you're counting heads.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does two years of warning give you, practically?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much. Two years isn't long enough to save anything on what I earn, and it's not long enough to learn a new trade from scratch. It's just long enough to watch it coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd look at teaching. Is that a real plan or a hope?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A hope, mostly. I've trained apprentices on the job for years, so I'm not starting from nothing. But a training centre job is one post for every fifty of us, and I'm not the only one who'd think of it.

S2.say: I'd say the government has to treat it as an emergency, regulate it and make companies pay into a fund for displaced workers. I'd go on a march, which I've only done twice in my life.
S2.think: I'd be sixty with almost nothing saved and a partner whose shop barely pays. If robots take the cable work there's no other firm to go to, and I don't know what we'd do.
S2.do: Goes through every household bill with her partner in the first month and gives up the car and the gym. Asks the union about redundancy terms, applies to teach the new kit at the training centre and joins a march.
S2.feel: Sick to her stomach, like counting heads after a pole goes down.
S2.quote: It's not long enough to learn a new trade from scratch. It's just long enough to watch it coming.
S2.fieldNote: Hana moves from steady to alarmed because her thin savings and a single local employer leave no fallback. She has a real lead on teaching but is honest that it's a long shot. Her politics turn from contract talks to street action.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got five years to get this right, so no excuses. Training, a fund, and a proper plan for older workers. I'd be pushing the branch to make that the main demand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years puts me at sixty-three. That's not long off retirement, and with five years I can at least get the teaching qualification and put a bit by. It still scares me, but it's a different kind of scared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sign up for the instructor course at the training centre in the first year, evenings, even if I had to pay part of it. I'd ask Ken for the rest of the loan over three years. And I'd try the newer AI tools for planning jobs, now that more people would be using them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but I'd feel like I was doing something about it, which helps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What changes most between two years and five for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In two years I'm reacting. In five, I'm preparing. That's the whole difference, and it's a big one for someone like me who likes to see a thing work before I jump.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about most at work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The younger women I've brought in. They fought to get into this trade and they'd be first out the door if the contractor shrinks. I'd want the union to make sure the last in aren't automatically the first out.

S3.say: I'd say five years means no excuses, and push the branch to make training, a fund and a plan for older workers the main demand.
S3.think: Five years puts me at sixty-three, close to retirement, with time to get a teaching qualification and save a little. It still scares me, but differently.
S3.do: Signs up for the evening instructor course at the training centre in the first year, paying part herself if needed. Asks her son to repay the rest of the loan over three years and starts trying AI planning tools as more colleagues use them.
S3.feel: Anxious but steadier, because she's doing something.
S3.quote: In two years I'm reacting. In five, I'm preparing.
S3.fieldNote: Five years suits her style exactly: time to see things proven before she commits. Her concern spreads to the younger women she brought into the trade. She wants the union to stop last-in-first-out cuts that would undo that progress.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the time to plan it like grown-ups. A decade is enough to retrain people properly and build a safety net. I'd say that at the branch, and I'd mean it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, I'd be sixty-eight. I'd have retired at sixty-six and the union pension would carry us, just about. It's the young ones in the trade I'd think about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working to sixty-six and spend the last few years teaching apprentices, formally if I can. I'd keep paying back our savings and help the branch push for retraining money. And I'd tell my daughter, who's twenty-nine, to pick her next move with all this in mind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly, and a bit sad for the trade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've talked a lot about others. What about you and Tomas?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd be all right, I think. Tomas says he'll fix bikes till he drops, and a robot isn't going to want his shop. With ten years, we'd have the loan back and a bit put away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you'd do differently now, knowing a decade was coming?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop putting off the teaching course. I keep saying next year. With a decade's notice I'd have no excuse.

S4.say: I'd say this is the time to plan it properly, because a decade is enough to retrain people and build a safety net. I'd say it at the branch and mean it.
S4.think: I'd be sixty-eight and retired at sixty-six, with the union pension carrying us just about. My thoughts go to the young people in the trade.
S4.do: Keeps working until sixty-six while teaching apprentices and finally signs up for the instructor course. Keeps rebuilding savings, pushes the branch for retraining money and tells her daughter to plan her next career move around it.
S4.feel: Mostly calm, with some sadness for the trade.
S4.quote: Tomas says he'll fix bikes till he drops, and a robot isn't going to want his shop.
S4.fieldNote: With ten years, Hana's own timeline sits safely before the change. She admits she keeps postponing the teaching course. Her partner's small shop gives her an odd kind of comfort.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. What would help is a fund, paid for by the companies that profit, that covers people like me until the pension starts. And funded places on instructor courses for older tradespeople, so our skills get passed on instead of thrown out.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask about the women. It took us twenty years to get a few of us into this trade. I don't want a robot to undo that in two, and nobody's even counting.

headlineQuote: It took us twenty years to get a few of us into this trade. I don't want a robot to undo that in two, and nobody's even counting.
portrait: Hana Ito is a fifty-eight-year-old cable jointer and lineworker for a lower-paid contractor in a river city, and the women's rep for her union branch. She lent most of the family savings to her divorced son, leaving about two weeks in the bank, and her partner's bike shop barely pays. She uses AI now and then for reports and adopts new tools once a trusted colleague has proven them. She is calm when AI fizzles, uneasy with steady change and alarmed by AGI in two years, when there would be nowhere else to work. More warning time turns her from reacting to preparing, mainly through a teaching qualification.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because she'd be sixty with almost no savings and no other cable firm nearby.
whatWouldHelp: A company-funded fund to cover older workers until their pension, and funded instructor courses so tradespeople can pass on their skills.
